claims.text: At 800–900 °C, FeNiCrCoCu coating wear resistance is predominantly governed by rapid formation of a continuous, adherent mixed oxide layer.
The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating is nanocrystalline.
Heating FeNiCrCoCu coatings in air at 800 °C can produce a controlled oxide scale before wear testing.
A load of approximately 26 N for 900 s is representative of the intended high-temperature service environment.
The surface film is a mixed oxide containing Fe, Ni, Co, and Cr oxides.
Cu oxide formation or Cu segregation may contribute to the surface-film behavior.
Selective oxidation of FeNiCrCoCu constituents occurs at elevated temperature.
Selective oxidation produces an in-situ protective oxide layer.
The oxide layer reduces direct metal-to-metal contact.
The oxide layer lowers friction.
Reduced contact and friction mitigate severe abrasive and adhesive wear.
Pre-oxidized FeNiCrCoCu coatings will have significantly less wear than as-deposited coatings during otherwise identical high-temperature tests.
Pre-oxidized FeNiCrCoCu coatings will have a lower coefficient of friction than as-deposited coatings.
The hypothesis is limited to oxidizing atmospheres at 800–900 °C.
Wear behavior at lower temperatures or in inert atmospheres may differ.
The oxide scale's precise composition, phase stability, and mechanical properties are not established for this alloy system.
Prior high-temperature wear studies on this specific FeNiCrCoCu coating system are limited.
A comparison of pre-oxidized and as-deposited coatings under identical wear conditions is the proposed test of the hypothesis.
Failure of pre-oxidation to reduce wear and friction is proposed as a falsifying result.
Failure to observe a continuous oxide film after pre-oxidation is proposed as a falsifying result.

contradictions.description: The outcome is called wear depth, but the example unit mm³/(N·m) denotes specific volumetric wear rate rather than depth.
